title: Philosophy of Science: What Makes Science Science?

questions.question: The demarcation problem asks:
options: How to divide the sciences into departments
questions.rationale: Demarcation is the question Popper made famous: what separates genuine science from pseudo-science? His answer - falsifiability - remains the most cited criterion in exams and courtrooms (including creation-science rulings).

questions.question: Popper's criterion of scientific status is:
options: Falsifiability - a theory must forbid some possible observation
questions.rationale: For Popper, a theory is scientific only if it risks refutation: 'all swans are white' is scientific because one black swan kills it. Verificationism (the positivists' earlier answer) fails because pseudo-theories can also accumulate confirming instances.

questions.question: The Duhem-Quine thesis undermines simple falsificationism by arguing that:
options: Hypotheses face evidence as a corporate body - a failed prediction might indict an auxiliary assumption, not the core theory
Evidence is irrelevant to theory choice
questions.rationale: A prediction needs auxiliaries (instruments, background laws). When the Uranus orbit misbehaved, astronomers fixed Newton by discovering Neptune rather than abandoning the core. Hence scientists rationally retain theories through anomalies.

questions.question: Kuhn's 'normal science' refers to:
options: Puzzle-solving research within an accepted paradigm
questions.rationale: Normal science fills in the paradigm's map - extending it, refining constants, solving its puzzles - until anomalies accumulate into crisis and a revolutionary paradigm shift occurs (Ptolemaic to Copernican, Newtonian to relativistic).

questions.question: Lakatos's research programmes consist of:
options: A protected hard core plus a protective belt of adjustable auxiliary hypotheses
questions.rationale: Lakatos mediated Popper and Kuhn: the hard core (e.g., Newton's laws) is kept by methodological decision; the belt absorbs refutations. Programmes are judged by whether they predict novel facts (progressive) or only patch old ones (degenerating).

questions.question: The 'no miracles' argument supports:
options: Scientific realism - successful theories would be miracles unless approximately true
questions.rationale: Realists argue that the predictive success of mature theories is best explained by their being at least approximately true - electrons and genes being real. Anti-realists reply with the pessimistic meta-induction: past successful theories (phlogiston, ether) went false.

questions.question: Van Fraassen's constructive empiricism holds that science aims at:
options: Empirical adequacy - saving the observable phenomena - without commitment to unobservables
questions.rationale: For the constructive empiricist, accepting a theory means believing it is empirically adequate, not believing its electrons and fields exist. Realism's debates over unobservables become optional metaphysics.

questions.question: Hempel's covering-law (D-N) model explains an event by:
options: Subsuming it under general laws plus initial conditions
questions.rationale: Deduce the event from laws and boundary conditions - the deductive-nomological ideal. Its counterexamples (flagpole/shadow asymmetry, irrelevancies) pushed philosophers toward causal-mechanistic and unificationist accounts of explanation.

questions.question: Bayesian philosophy of science models rational belief using:
options: Probability - evidence raises a theory's posterior in proportion to predictive likelihood
questions.rationale: Bayesians update credences by conditionalisation: strong evidence for a theory is one it predicts much better than rivals. The approach powers today's statistics and the replication-crisis debates over p-values and priors.

questions.question: Feyerabend's position in 'Against Method' is captured by:
options: 'Anything goes' - no single methodology governs all good science
questions.rationale: Feyerabend argued history shows successful scientists breaking every proposed rule; methodological anarchism follows. He is the standard endpoint of the method debate: Popper's rules, Kuhn's history, Lakatos's programmes, then Feyerabend's shrug.
